site.name: dotyoujee / Ops Log
site.tagline: IT consultancy in Kampala. Cybersecurity apprenticeship in public.

tracks.title: Networking & Linux Foundations
tracks.short: The bedrock. Everything else sits on this.

modules.title: How a packet actually travels
objectives: Explain encapsulation from application data to frame
Read an OSI/TCP-IP map without confusing the two
Trace one DNS lookup and one HTTPS request end to end
modules.lab: Capture a single DNS query and TCP handshake in Wireshark; annotate every layer in a writeup.

modules.title: IPv4, subnetting and CIDR
objectives: Convert between binary, decimal and CIDR
Subnet a /24 into four equal networks
Explain why private ranges exist and where NAT breaks things
modules.lab: Subnet a fictional Kampala SACCO network with 4 branches; document addresses, gateways and broadcast domains.

modules.title: DNS, HTTP and TLS in practice
objectives: Walk through recursive DNS resolution
Read an HTTP response header line by line
Explain the TLS handshake and what a certificate proves
modules.lab: Use dig and openssl s_client against a domain you own or are authorised to test; save annotated output.

modules.title: Linux filesystem, users and permissions
objectives: Navigate the filesystem and explain FHS layout
Read and set rwx bits, setuid and sticky bits
Create users/groups and explain why least privilege matters
modules.lab: Build a shared folder with two groups and verify who can read, write and execute.

modules.title: Processes, services and systemd
objectives: List and inspect running processes
Explain signals, foreground and background jobs
Write a minimal systemd unit and read its journal
modules.lab: Run a small Python HTTP server as a systemd service; break it, then fix it from journalctl.

modules.title: Shell, piping and text tools
objectives: Compose grep, sed, awk and sort pipelines
Use find and xargs safely
Write a bash script with argument checks and exit codes
modules.lab: Write a script that parses auth.log and reports failed SSH logins per IP.

modules.title: Networking on Linux
objectives: Inspect interfaces with ip and ss
Read a routing table and add a static route
Explain iptables/nftables chains and a basic firewall policy
modules.lab: Configure two VMs on an isolated network, route between them, then block a port with nftables.

modules.title: Windows basics and Active Directory
objectives: Explain domains, OUs, users and groups
Describe what a domain controller does
Read a Group Policy and know what it enforces
modules.lab: Draw an AD topology for a 40-person SACCO and mark privileged groups.

modules.title: Logs, time and observability
objectives: Explain syslog severity and journald
Sync clocks with NTP and explain why time matters in incidents
Correlate two log sources into one timeline
modules.lab: Collect auth.log, journal and nginx logs for one day and write a timeline of a suspicious event.
resources: The Practice of Network Security Monitoring ch.2

modules.title: Boss fight: build the home lab
objectives: Stand up a repeatable lab from documented steps
Segment it into attacker, victim and management networks
Publish a build log with diagrams and failure notes
modules.lab: Document the whole build, including what broke and how you fixed it. Evidence link is mandatory.
resources: Your own notes from nl-01 to nl-09

tracks.title: Penetration Testing Journey
tracks.short: Authorised breaking, scoped properly, reported clearly.

modules.title: Rules of engagement and legal scope
objectives: Explain the difference between authorisation, consent and permission to test
Write a scope document that names in-scope assets, out-of-scope assets and test windows
Define stop conditions, emergency contacts and a data-handling plan
Describe the legal consequences of testing without written authorisation in Uganda and abroad
modules.lab: Using a template in a text editor, draft a one-page RoE for a fictional Kampala SACCO web app: name the asset list, permitted techniques, exclusions, test window, stop conditions and named contacts. Save it as a Markdown file in a git repo and publish the commit link as evidence.
resources: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide v4 - pre-engagement interactions (free)
NIST SP 800-115 - Information Security Testing and Assessment (free)

modules.title: Host discovery and scanning with Nmap
objectives: Explain what -sS, -sT, -sV, -sC, -O and -Pn change about a scan and when each is appropriate
Interpret service versions, OS guesses and script output without trusting them blindly
Keep scan traffic inside an authorised scope and respect rate and timing limits
Turn a raw port list into a short target-priority note
modules.lab: Against a VM you own in an isolated lab, run `nmap -sS -sV -sC -O -oA pt02-scan <target-ip>` and a targeted `nmap -p 80,443 --script http-title -oN pt02-web.nmap <target-ip>`. Write a short writeup that explains three open ports and one false positive, and link the saved .nmap/.gnmap artefacts as evidence.
resources: Nmap Network Scanning book - online chapters (free)
RFC 793 and RFC 9293 for the TCP handshake behaviour

modules.title: Web fundamentals and the OWASP Top 10
objectives: Trace how a browser request becomes a server response, including cookies, sessions and same-origin policy
Map at least five findings to the current OWASP Top 10 categories with a concrete example each
Demonstrate impact safely: read or modify only your own test data, never real user records
Distinguish a confirmed vulnerability from a theoretical one and record what evidence proves it
modules.lab: Stand up OWASP Juice Shop locally (`docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop`) and use only the browser plus DevTools to confirm one broken-access-control and one injection finding. Save screenshots of the request/response and write a short writeup mapping each to an OWASP Top 10 category; commit the evidence to a repo.
resources: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide v4 (free)
MDN Web Docs: HTTP, cookies and same-origin policy (free)

modules.title: Burp Suite and authenticated testing
objectives: Configure Burp Suite Community Edition as a browser proxy and install its CA certificate in a lab browser
Use Proxy, Target and Repeater to capture, inspect and replay a request
Maintain an authenticated session in a tool without sharing or leaking real credentials
Test access control by swapping identifiers between two test accounts you control
modules.lab: Proxy a local Juice Shop or DVWA session through `burpsuite` Community Edition, add the lab host to scope, log in as two throwaway accounts, and use Repeater to swap the user/ID parameter between them. Save the request/response screenshots plus a note on the broken access control as an evidence writeup in a repo.
resources: PortSwigger Web Security Academy - Burp Suite basics (free)
OWASP Testing Guide - authentication and authorization testing (free)

modules.title: API testing basics
objectives: Describe the common REST request methods, status codes and JSON payload shapes
Read an OpenAPI/Swagger definition to enumerate endpoints and parameters
Test object-level and function-level authorization by changing IDs and roles in your own lab
Explain why APIs need separate tests from the browser front end
modules.lab: Against a local API you control (e.g. `docker run -p 80:80 vulnapi/crapi` in an isolated VM), fetch `/openapi.json` or the Swagger UI, replay a few endpoints with `curl -i -X <method>` and use Burp Repeater to change an object ID between two test users. Save the OpenAPI file, the curl output and a short findings writeup as repo evidence.
resources: OWASP Web Security Testing Guide - web service testing (free)

modules.title: Vulnerability validation and CVSS
objectives: Reproduce a finding with a minimal, repeatable sequence of steps
Calculate a CVSS v3.1 base score and explain what the metrics mean
Adjust severity for business context rather than quoting a score blindly
Write a finding with evidence, impact, affected asset and a realistic remediation
modules.lab: Take three findings from your pt-03 to pt-05 labs and, using the FIRST CVSS v3.1 calculator, record a base score and vector for each plus one business-context note. Produce a Markdown findings register with steps-to-reproduce and screenshots, and commit it as evidence.
resources: FIRST CVSS v3.1 specification and calculator (first.org, free)

modules.title: Linux privilege escalation basics
objectives: Explain the difference between vertical and horizontal privilege escalation
Find misconfigured file permissions, SUID binaries and scheduled jobs in a lab VM
Read a sudoers file and understand why overly broad rules are dangerous
Tie each finding back to a concrete hardening action
modules.lab: In a disposable Linux VM you own, run `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` and `sudo -l` as a low-privilege user, inspect `/etc/crontab` and world-writable files, then document how one misconfigurable permission could be abused. Save the exact commands, their output and a remediation note as a writeup with linked screenshots.

modules.title: Active Directory attack path fundamentals (defensive framing)
objectives: Describe domains, forests, trusts, OUs and the role of a domain controller
Explain in defensive terms how Kerberos authentication and ticket requests work
Read an ACL or group membership chain and spot why excessive privilege is risky
Map a common attack path to a specific detection and a hardening control
modules.lab: Using a Windows evaluation VM with a local AD domain you set up, or a prebuilt lab VM, draw a topology with Domain Admins, a service account and a workstation, then use `net user /domain`, `net group "Domain Admins" /domain` and a Group Policy report to document one over-privileged path. Write a defensive review that names the risk, a detection source (e.g. event ID 4768/4769) and the fix; save the diagram and notes as evidence.
resources: Mandiant/Microsoft AD attack map - defensive reading (free)
MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise - Active Directory techniques (free)

modules.title: Boss fight: full scoped web app assessment
objectives: Produce a signed RoE and scope before touching a target
Run a complete assessment from reconnaissance through authenticated and API testing
Write a client-ready report with validated findings, CVSS scores and remediation
Perform a retest after fixes and record which findings are resolved
modules.lab: Take an authorised lab web app end to end: write the RoE, scan with `nmap -sV -sC -oA pt09-<app>`, test via Burp and curl, validate findings with CVSS, and deliver a report plus a retest log. Publish the RoE, redacted evidence, report and retest results as a linked writeup/repo so the whole engagement is verifiable.
resources: Your own notes from pt-01 through pt-08
OWASP Web Security Testing Guide v4 (free)

tracks.title: Reverse Engineering Journey
tracks.short: Binaries, assembly and how software really behaves.

modules.title: CPU registers and the stack
objectives: Name the x86-64 general-purpose registers and explain the roles of RSP, RBP, RIP and RFLAGS
Draw the stack layout for a function call showing the saved return address and local variables
Explain little-endian byte order when reading a hex dump of a 64-bit value
modules.lab: In a 64-bit Linux VM compile a 10-line C program with gcc -g -O0 and inspect it with objdump -d -M intel and readelf -a; save an annotated screenshot of the stack pointer changes and frame layout as re01-stack-notes.md.
resources: Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual Vol. 1
Linux Journey: the shell and processes

modules.title: Reading assembly with objdump
objectives: Translate common x86-64 instructions (mov, lea, push/pop, call/ret, cmp/test and jcc) into plain English
Switch objdump between Intel and AT&T syntax with -M intel and explain the difference
Locate main and a helper function in an objdump listing from their prologue and epilogue
modules.lab: Run objdump -d -M intel ./target | less on a self-compiled binary and produce a line-by-line annotated disassembly of two functions; save it as re02-objdump-annotations.md.
resources: Intel SDM Vol. 2 instruction set reference
x86-64 Assembly Language Programming with Ubuntu (free PDF)

modules.title: C compilation and calling conventions
objectives: Describe the System V AMD64 calling convention: argument registers, return value and caller-versus-callee-saved registers
Predict which register holds each of the first six integer arguments at a call site
Explain what -O0 versus -O2 changes in a disassembly and why optimisation level matters when reversing
modules.lab: Compile the same C file with gcc -O0 and gcc -O2, diff the objdump -d -M intel output with diff -u, and write a one-page explanation saved as re03-calling-convention.md.

modules.title: Ghidra static analysis
objectives: Import a binary into Ghidra and run Auto Analysis
Rename functions and variables and add comments so the decompiled C matches your objdump reading
Follow cross-references from a string in the data section to the code that uses it
modules.lab: Import a self-written key-check program into Ghidra, decompile main, rename and comment the key logic, and export annotated screenshots as re04-ghidra-annotations.md.
resources: Ghidra official documentation and cheat sheet

modules.title: Dynamic analysis with gdb
objectives: Set breakpoints and step with si and ni while inspecting registers and memory in gdb
Compare what Ghidra predicted statically with the values observed at runtime
Use the gdb x/ command to examine stack and heap bytes and explain what they represent
modules.lab: Debug a self-compiled key-check program with gdb -q ./crackme, break at the comparison instruction, run info registers and x/s $rsp, and save the full transcript as re05-gdb-session.txt.

modules.title: Crackmes and key checks
objectives: Recognise common key-check patterns: strcmp chains, arithmetic checks and length checks
Patch a conditional jump and explain the behavioural difference it causes
Recover the valid serial and document the check logic without publishing a working keygen
modules.lab: Solve one beginner crackme from crackmes.one inside the isolated no-network VM, document the check logic and the patched bytes with xxd output, and save it as re06-crackme-writeup.md.
resources: Ghidra plus gdb combined workflow notes

modules.title: Packing and unpacking in an isolated VM
objectives: Explain what a packer does and why malware uses it, purely in a defensive analysis context
Identify a packed binary through section names, high entropy and a thin import table
Dump an unpacked sample from memory safely and hash both the packed and unpacked stages
modules.lab: In a no-network snapshot VM inspect a harmless packed test binary with Detect It Easy (DIE), file, strings and sha256sum, record both stage hashes and save the findings as re07-unpack-notes.md.
resources: REMnux and Flare VM lab documentation

modules.title: Basic malware behaviour analysis and IOCs
objectives: Observe a safe test sample's process, file, registry and network behaviour inside a sandbox
Extract useful IOCs: hashes, IPs and domains, file paths and mutex names
Write a short behaviour report that clearly separates direct observation from inference
modules.lab: Run a harmless test sample in an isolated REMnux/Flare VM, capture activity with procmon, Wireshark and Sysmon, and save an IOC table plus findings as re08-behaviour-report.md.

modules.title: Boss fight: full reverse-engineering writeup of a safe sample
objectives: Combine static and dynamic analysis into one coherent, reproducible narrative
Produce a behaviour report with a defensible IOC list
Publish a clean writeup that another apprentice can follow and learn from
Keep every step inside the isolated lab and state the safety controls used
modules.lab: In a fully isolated, no-network snapshot VM reverse a self-authored or CTF-provided safe sample end to end and publish re09-full-writeup.md containing disassembly, annotated Ghidra screenshots, a gdb transcript, a behaviour report and an IOC table.
resources: Your notes from re-01 through re-08
MITRE ATT&CK for mapping observed behaviour
